claim: Predator-prey interactions influence prey traits through both consumptive and non-consumptive effects.
source: Predator-prey interactions influence prey traits through both consumptive and non-consumptive effects, and variation in these traits can shape vector-borne disease dynamics.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the entire meta-analysis study presented in the manuscript.

claim: Variation in prey traits can shape vector-borne disease dynamics.
source: Predator-prey interactions influence prey traits through both consumptive and non-consumptive effects, and variation in these traits can shape vector-borne disease dynamics.
evidence: This statement is supported by the discussion of how vector traits affect disease transmission throughout the manuscript.

claim: Multiple families of aquatic predators are effective in consumptively reducing mosquito survival.
source: This analysis showed that multiple families of aquatic predators are effective in consumptively reducing mosquito survival, and that the survival of Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex mosquitoes is negatively impacted by consumptive effects of predators.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results showing significant effects across multiple predator families.

claim: The survival of Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex mosquitoes is negatively impacted by consumptive effects of predators.
source: This analysis showed that multiple families of aquatic predators are effective in consumptively reducing mosquito survival, and that the survival of Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex mosquitoes is negatively impacted by consumptive effects of predators.
evidence: This is directly supported by the meta-analysis data presented in Figure 3b.

claim: Mosquito larval size plays a more important role in explaining the heterogeneity of consumptive effects from predators than mosquito genus.
source: Mosquito larval size was found to play a more important role in explaining the heterogeneity of consumptive effects from predators than mosquito genus.
evidence: This is supported by the AICc model comparison showing that larval instar (indicator of size) had better model fit than genus.

claim: Mosquito survival is reduced by non-consumptive effects of predators.
source: Mosquito survival and body size were reduced by non-consumptive effects of predators, but development time was not significantly impacted.
evidence: This is supported by the random effects model showing an effect size of -0.11 for non-consumptive survival effects.

claim: Mosquito body size is reduced by non-consumptive effects of predators.
source: Mosquito survival and body size were reduced by non-consumptive effects of predators, but development time was not significantly impacted.
evidence: This is supported by the random effects model results showing significant negative effects on both male and female body size.

claim: Mosquito development time is not significantly impacted by non-consumptive effects of predators.
source: Mosquito survival and body size were reduced by non-consumptive effects of predators, but development time was not significantly impacted.
evidence: This is supported by the random effects model results showing non-significant effects on development time for both sexes.

claim: Culex vectors demonstrate predator avoidance behavior during oviposition.
source: In addition, Culex vectors demonstrated predator avoidance behavior during oviposition.
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analysis results showing significant negative effect size for Culex oviposition in presence of predators.

claim: Predators limit disease transmission by reducing both vector survival and vector size.
source: The results of this meta-analysis suggest that predators limit disease transmission by reducing both vector survival and vector size, and that associations between drought and human West Nile virus cases could be driven by the vector behavior of predator avoidance during oviposition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analysis results combined with knowledge of disease transmission dynamics.

claim: Associations between drought and human West Nile virus cases could be driven by the vector behavior of predator avoidance during oviposition.
source: The results of this meta-analysis suggest that predators limit disease transmission by reducing both vector survival and vector size, and that associations between drought and human West Nile virus cases could be driven by the vector behavior of predator avoidance during oviposition.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed oviposition avoidance behavior in Culex mosquitoes.

claim: Predation reduces vector populations through consumptive effects.
source: While it is well known that predation reduces vector populations through consumptive effects, non-consumptive effects of predators can also greatly impact prey demographics (Preisser et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Non-consumptive effects of predators can greatly impact prey demographics.
source: While it is well known that predation reduces vector populations through consumptive effects, non-consumptive effects of predators can also greatly impact prey demographics (Preisser et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Preisser et al., 2005.

claim: Mosquitoes are vectors of malaria, lymphatic filariasis, chikungunya, Zika, and dengue.
source: Mosquitoes are vectors of a variety of debilitating and deadly diseases, including malaria, lymphatic filariasis, and arboviruses, such as chikungunya, Zika, and dengue (Weaver and Reisen, 2010; WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Incorporation of vector trait variation into disease models can improve the reliability of their predictions.
source: In addition, recent work has suggested that incorporation of vector trait variation into disease models can improve the reliability of their predictions (Cator et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cator et al., 2020.

claim: Mosquito insecticide resistance is recognized as a growing problem.
source: Mosquito insecticide resistance is recognized as a growing problem (Hancock et al., 2018; Hemingway and Ranson, 2000; Liu, 2015) leading some to suggest that control efforts should rely more heavily on 'non-insecticide based strategies' (Benelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some suggest that mosquito control efforts should rely more heavily on non-insecticide based strategies.
source: Mosquito insecticide resistance is recognized as a growing problem (Hancock et al., 2018; Hemingway and Ranson, 2000; Liu, 2015) leading some to suggest that control efforts should rely more heavily on 'non-insecticide based strategies' (Benelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benelli et al., 2016.

claim: Cyclopoid copepods have been used for mosquito biocontrol purposes.
source: Past biocontrol efforts have used predators such as cyclopoid copepods (Kay et al., 2002; Marten, 1990; Russell et al., 1996; Veronesi et al., 2015) and mosquitofish (Pyke, 2008, Seale, 1917) to target the mosquito's aquatic larval stage.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting past biocontrol efforts.

claim: Mosquitofish have been used for mosquito biocontrol purposes.
source: Past biocontrol efforts have used predators such as cyclopoid copepods (Kay et al., 2002; Marten, 1990; Russell et al., 1996; Veronesi et al., 2015) and mosquitofish (Pyke, 2008, Seale, 1917) to target the mosquito's aquatic larval stage.
evidence: This is supported by citations documenting past biocontrol efforts.

claim: Predator-prey body size ratios tend to be higher in freshwater habitats than other types of habitats.
source: Predator-prey body size ratios tend to be higher in freshwater habitats than other types of habitats (Brose et al., 2006), and attack rate tends to increase with temperature (Kalinoski and DeLong, 2016; Dam and Peterson, 1988), although other studies suggest a unimodal response to temperature (Uiterwaal and Delong, 2020; Englund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brose et al., 2006.

claim: Attack rate tends to increase with temperature.
source: Predator-prey body size ratios tend to be higher in freshwater habitats than other types of habitats (Brose et al., 2006), and attack rate tends to increase with temperature (Kalinoski and DeLong, 2016; Dam and Peterson, 1988), although other studies suggest a unimodal response to temperature (Uiterwaal and Delong, 2020; Englund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kalinoski and DeLong, 2016 and Dam and Peterson, 1988.

claim: Some studies suggest a unimodal response of attack rate to temperature.
source: Predator-prey body size ratios tend to be higher in freshwater habitats than other types of habitats (Brose et al., 2006), and attack rate tends to increase with temperature (Kalinoski and DeLong, 2016; Dam and Peterson, 1988), although other studies suggest a unimodal response to temperature (Uiterwaal and Delong, 2020; Englund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uiterwaal and Delong, 2020 and Englund et al., 2011.

claim: Non-consumptive effects of predators are thought to be more pronounced in aquatic ecosystems than in terrestrial ecosystems.
source: Predators can also have non-consumptive effects on prey (Peacor and Werner, 2001), and these effects are thought to be more pronounced in aquatic ecosystems than in terrestrial ecosystems (Preisser et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Preisser et al., 2005.

claim: Non-consumptive effects of predators result from prey initiating anti-predator behavioral and/or physiological trait changes.
source: Non-consumptive effects of predators are the result of the prey initiating anti-predator behavioral and/or physiological trait changes that can aid in predator avoidance (Hermann and Landis, 2017; Lima and Dill, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hermann and Landis, 2017 and Lima and Dill, 1990.

claim: Plasticity in prey traits may result in energetic costs.
source: Such plasticity in certain prey traits may also result in energetic costs (Lima, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lima, 1998.

claim: Predator detection can be mediated by chemical, tactile, and visual cues.
source: Predator detection is key for these trait changes to occur and can be mediated by chemical, tactile, and visual cues (Hermann and Thaler, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hermann and Thaler, 2014.

claim: Exposure to predators affects mosquito behavior, size, development, and survival.
source: In mosquitoes, exposure to predators is known to affect a variety of traits including behavior, size, development, and survival (Arav and Blaustein, 2006; Bond et al., 2005; Roberts, 2012; Roux et al., 2015, Zuharah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Experimental observations of predator effects on mosquito size and development are inconsistent.
source: Experimental observations of predator effects on mosquito size and development are inconsistent and results sometimes vary by mosquito sex.
evidence: This is supported by the examples provided in the following sentences citing contradictory findings.

claim: Exposure to predation increases the size of Culex pipiens mosquitoes.
source: For example, exposure to predation was found to increase the size of Culex pipiens mosquitoes (Alcalay et al., 2018) but decrease the size of Culiseta longiareolata (Stav et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alcalay et al., 2018.

claim: Exposure to predation decreases the size of Culiseta longiareolata.
source: For example, exposure to predation was found to increase the size of Culex pipiens mosquitoes (Alcalay et al., 2018) but decrease the size of Culiseta longiareolata (Stav et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stav et al., 2005.

claim: Female Aedes triseriatus exhibit shorter development times when exposed to predation at high nutrient availability.
source: In addition, female Aedes triseriatus exhibited shorter development times when exposed to predation at high nutrient availability (Ower and Juliano, 2019), but male C. longiareolata had longer development times in the presence of predators (Stav et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ower and Juliano, 2019.

claim: Male Culiseta longiareolata have longer development times in the presence of predators.
source: In addition, female Aedes triseriatus exhibited shorter development times when exposed to predation at high nutrient availability (Ower and Juliano, 2019), but male C. longiareolata had longer development times in the presence of predators (Stav et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stav et al., 2005.

claim: A shared evolutionary history between predator and prey organisms can strengthen the non-consumptive effects of predators on mosquitoes.
source: In some cases, a shared evolutionary history between predator and prey organisms can strengthen the non-consumptive effects of predators on mosquitoes (Buchanan et al., 2017; Sih, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buchanan et al., 2017 and Sih, 1986.

claim: Non-consumptive effects of predators are expected to cause a smaller reduction in mosquito survival than consumptive effects.
source: Non-consumptive effects of predators are expected to cause a smaller reduction in mosquito survival than consumptive effects because, in practice, measures of consumptive effects always include both consumptive and non-consumptive effects.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the practical constraints of experimental design.

claim: Larger predators are more likely to consumptively reduce mosquito survival.
source: Based on previous findings, larger predators are more likely to consumptively reduce mosquito survival (Kumar et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2008.

claim: Aedes mosquito larvae may be more vulnerable to consumption than other genera because of the high degree of motility observed in this genus.
source: In addition, Aedes mosquito larvae may be more vulnerable to consumption than other genera because of the high degree of motility observed in this genus (Dieng et al., 2003; Marten and Reid, 2007; Soumare and Cilek, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting Aedes motility.

claim: The oviposition response to predation is expected to be weakest among Aedes species that oviposit above the water line.
source: The oviposition response to predation is expected to be weakest among Aedes species that oviposit above the water line, due in part to their delayed-hatching eggs (Vonesh and Blaustein, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vonesh and Blaustein, 2010.

claim: Predation is predicted to reduce mosquito size and lengthen development time.
source: Predation is predicted to reduce mosquito size and lengthen development time, consistent with the reduced growth response observed in other insect systems (Hermann and Landis, 2017).
evidence: This is a prediction based on citation to Hermann and Landis, 2017.

claim: A systematic search was conducted for studies on predation of mosquitoes published between 1970 and July 1, 2019.
source: A systematic search was conducted for studies on predation of mosquitoes that were published between 1970 and July 1, 2019 using both PubMed and Web of Science search engines, according to the PRISMA protocol (Moher et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: 306 studies were fully reviewed after abstract screening.
source: This resulted in 306 studies that were fully reviewed to determine if any predation data could be extracted (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The final database comprised data extracted from 60 studies.
source: The final database comprised data extracted from 60 studies (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the analysis.

claim: Predators consumptively decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of -1.23.
source: Random effects model results showed that predators consumptively decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of –1.23 (95% CI −1.43,–1.03), p-value < 0.0001, and non-consumptively reduced survival with a smaller effect size of –0.11 (95% CI −0.17,–0.04), p-value = 0.0016.
evidence: This is a direct result from the random effects model analysis.

claim: Predators non-consumptively reduced mosquito survival with an effect size of -0.11.
source: Random effects model results showed that predators consumptively decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of –1.23 (95% CI −1.43,–1.03), p-value < 0.0001, and non-consumptively reduced survival with a smaller effect size of –0.11 (95% CI −0.17,–0.04), p-value = 0.0016.
evidence: This is a direct result from the random effects model analysis.

claim: Predators non-consumptively reduced oviposition behavior with an effect size of -0.87.
source: In addition, predators non-consumptively reduced oviposition behavior with an effect size of –0.87 (95% CI −1.31,–0.42), p-value = 0.0001, and mosquito body size was non-consumptively reduced by predators in both males and females; the female effect size was –0.13 (95% CI −0.19,–0.06), p-value = 0.0002, and the male effect size was –0.03 (95% CI −0.06,–0.01), p-value = 0.0184.
evidence: This is a direct result from the random effects model analysis.

claim: Mosquito body size was non-consumptively reduced by predators in females with an effect size of -0.13.
source: In addition, predators non-consumptively reduced oviposition behavior with an effect size of –0.87 (95% CI −1.31,–0.42), p-value = 0.0001, and mosquito body size was non-consumptively reduced by predators in both males and females; the female effect size was –0.13 (95% CI −0.19,–0.06), p-value = 0.0002, and the male effect size was –0.03 (95% CI −0.06,–0.01), p-value = 0.0184.
evidence: This is a direct result from the random effects model analysis.

claim: Mosquito body size was non-consumptively reduced by predators in males with an effect size of -0.03.
source: In addition, predators non-consumptively reduced oviposition behavior with an effect size of –0.87 (95% CI −1.31,–0.42), p-value = 0.0001, and mosquito body size was non-consumptively reduced by predators in both males and females; the female effect size was –0.13 (95% CI −0.19,–0.06), p-value = 0.0002, and the male effect size was –0.03 (95% CI −0.06,–0.01), p-value = 0.0184.
evidence: This is a direct result from the random effects model analysis.

claim: There was not a significant non-consumptive effect of predators on female development time.
source: There was not a significant non-consumptive effect of predators on either male or female development time; the female effect size was –0.01 (95% CI –0.09, 0.07), p-value = 0.7901, and the male effect size was –0.04 (95% CI –0.12, 0.04), p-value = 0.3273.
evidence: This is a direct result from the random effects model analysis showing non-significant p-value.

claim: There was not a significant non-consumptive effect of predators on male development time.
source: There was not a significant non-consumptive effect of predators on either male or female development time; the female effect size was –0.01 (95% CI –0.09, 0.07), p-value = 0.7901, and the male effect size was –0.04 (95% CI –0.12, 0.04), p-value = 0.3273.
evidence: This is a direct result from the random effects model analysis showing non-significant p-value.

claim: Cyprinidae predators decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of -3.44.
source: Predator families that decreased mosquito survival included Cyprinidae: –3.44 (95% CI −5.79,–1.09), p-value = 0.0042; Poeciliidae: –1.42 (95% CI −2.67,–0.16), p-value = 0.0270; Ambystomatidae: –5.18 (95% CI −7.94,–2.42), p-value = 0.0002; Aeshnidae: –2.93 (95% CI −4.80,–1.07), p-value = 0.0020; and Notonectidae: –2.14 (95% CI −3.07,–1.21), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Poeciliidae predators decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of -1.42.
source: Predator families that decreased mosquito survival included Cyprinidae: –3.44 (95% CI −5.79,–1.09), p-value = 0.0042; Poeciliidae: –1.42 (95% CI −2.67,–0.16), p-value = 0.0270; Ambystomatidae: –5.18 (95% CI −7.94,–2.42), p-value = 0.0002; Aeshnidae: –2.93 (95% CI −4.80,–1.07), p-value = 0.0020; and Notonectidae: –2.14 (95% CI −3.07,–1.21), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Ambystomatidae predators decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of -5.18.
source: Predator families that decreased mosquito survival included Cyprinidae: –3.44 (95% CI −5.79,–1.09), p-value = 0.0042; Poeciliidae: –1.42 (95% CI −2.67,–0.16), p-value = 0.0270; Ambystomatidae: –5.18 (95% CI −7.94,–2.42), p-value = 0.0002; Aeshnidae: –2.93 (95% CI −4.80,–1.07), p-value = 0.0020; and Notonectidae: –2.14 (95% CI −3.07,–1.21), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Aeshnidae predators decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of -2.93.
source: Predator families that decreased mosquito survival included Cyprinidae: –3.44 (95% CI −5.79,–1.09), p-value = 0.0042; Poeciliidae: –1.42 (95% CI −2.67,–0.16), p-value = 0.0270; Ambystomatidae: –5.18 (95% CI −7.94,–2.42), p-value = 0.0002; Aeshnidae: –2.93 (95% CI −4.80,–1.07), p-value = 0.0020; and Notonectidae: –2.14 (95% CI −3.07,–1.21), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Notonectidae predators decreased mosquito survival with an effect size of -2.14.
source: Predator families that decreased mosquito survival included Cyprinidae: –3.44 (95% CI −5.79,–1.09), p-value = 0.0042; Poeciliidae: –1.42 (95% CI −2.67,–0.16), p-value = 0.0270; Ambystomatidae: –5.18 (95% CI −7.94,–2.42), p-value = 0.0002; Aeshnidae: –2.93 (95% CI −4.80,–1.07), p-value = 0.0020; and Notonectidae: –2.14 (95% CI −3.07,–1.21), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Aedes mosquitoes experienced significant decreases in survival due to consumptive effects of predators with an effect size of -1.23.
source: Vector genera that experienced significant decreases in survival due to consumptive effects of predators included Aedes: –1.23 (95% CI −1.81,–0.65), p-value < 0.0001; Anopheles: –1.34 (95% CI −2.01,–0.66), p-value = 0.0001; and Culex: –1.41 (95% CI −1.96,–0.86), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Anopheles mosquitoes experienced significant decreases in survival due to consumptive effects of predators with an effect size of -1.34.
source: Vector genera that experienced significant decreases in survival due to consumptive effects of predators included Aedes: –1.23 (95% CI −1.81,–0.65), p-value < 0.0001; Anopheles: –1.34 (95% CI −2.01,–0.66), p-value = 0.0001; and Culex: –1.41 (95% CI −1.96,–0.86), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Culex mosquitoes experienced significant decreases in survival due to consumptive effects of predators with an effect size of -1.41.
source: Vector genera that experienced significant decreases in survival due to consumptive effects of predators included Aedes: –1.23 (95% CI −1.81,–0.65), p-value < 0.0001; Anopheles: –1.34 (95% CI −2.01,–0.66), p-value = 0.0001; and Culex: –1.41 (95% CI −1.96,–0.86), p-value < 0.0001 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the multilevel mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The best model fit for consumptive survival data was achieved when an interaction between predator family and vector genus was included.
source: Among all 187 consumptive survival observations from 34 studies, the best model fit, according to AICc value, was achieved when an interaction between predator family and vector genus was included in the model (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on AICc model comparison shown in Table 2.

claim: Among larval stage observations, adding an interactive term between larval instar and predator family had a greater improvement on model fit than adding an interactive term between vector genus and predator family.
source: However, among the 163 larval stage consumptive survival observations from 30 studies, adding an interactive term between larval instar (an indicator of prey size) and predator family had a greater improvement on model fit than adding an interactive term between vector genus and predator family (Figure 3c, Table 3).
evidence: This is based on AICc model comparison shown in Table 3.

claim: Temperature did not affect the heterogeneity of consumptive survival data as a linear moderator.
source: Temperature did not affect the heterogeneity of consumptive survival data, either as a linear moderator: –0.01 (95% CI –0.10, 0.07), p-value = 0.7559, or a quadratic moderator: 0.00 (95% CI 0.00, 0.00), p-value = 0.8184.
evidence: This is based on multilevel mixed effects model results showing non-significant p-values.

claim: Temperature did not affect the heterogeneity of consumptive survival data as a quadratic moderator.
source: Temperature did not affect the heterogeneity of consumptive survival data, either as a linear moderator: –0.01 (95% CI –0.10, 0.07), p-value = 0.7559, or a quadratic moderator: 0.00 (95% CI 0.00, 0.00), p-value = 0.8184.
evidence: This is based on multilevel mixed effects model results showing non-significant p-values.

claim: The best oviposition model fit was achieved when vector genus was added as a moderator.
source: The best oviposition model fit, according to AICc value, was achieved when vector genus was added as a moderator (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on AICc model comparison shown in Table 4.

claim: The mean oviposition effect size was not significantly different than zero for Aedes.
source: The mean oviposition effect size was not significantly different than zero for Aedes: 0.32 (95% CI –2.14, 2.79), p-value = 0.7970, or Culiseta: –0.61 (95% CI –1.83, 0.62), p-value = 0.3329, but for Culex mosquitoes, oviposition was significantly decreased by predator presence: –1.69 (95% CI −2.82,–0.56), p-value = 0.0033 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on multilevel mixed effects model results showing non-significant p-value.

claim: The mean oviposition effect size was not significantly different than zero for Culiseta.
source: The mean oviposition effect size was not significantly different than zero for Aedes: 0.32 (95% CI –2.14, 2.79), p-value = 0.7970, or Culiseta: –0.61 (95% CI –1.83, 0.62), p-value = 0.3329, but for Culex mosquitoes, oviposition was significantly decreased by predator presence: –1.69 (95% CI −2.82,–0.56), p-value = 0.0033 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on multilevel mixed effects model results showing non-significant p-value.

claim: For Culex mosquitoes, oviposition was significantly decreased by predator presence with an effect size of -1.69.
source: The mean oviposition effect size was not significantly different than zero for Aedes: 0.32 (95% CI –2.14, 2.79), p-value = 0.7970, or Culiseta: –0.61 (95% CI –1.83, 0.62), p-value = 0.3329, but for Culex mosquitoes, oviposition was significantly decreased by predator presence: –1.69 (95% CI −2.82,–0.56), p-value = 0.0033 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on multilevel mixed effects model results showing significant p-value.

claim: Exposure of mosquito larvae to predation is commonplace in outdoor field settings.
source: Although exposure of mosquito larvae to predators is commonplace in outdoor field settings, it remains rare in most laboratory-based assessments of vector traits.
evidence: This is a general observation about field versus laboratory conditions.

claim: Exposure of mosquito larvae to predators remains rare in most laboratory-based assessments of vector traits.
source: Although exposure of mosquito larvae to predators is commonplace in outdoor field settings, it remains rare in most laboratory-based assessments of vector traits.
evidence: This is a general observation about laboratory practices.

claim: Mosquitoes observed in nature are likely to have smaller body sizes than those observed under optimal laboratory conditions.
source: Therefore, mosquitoes observed in nature are likely to have smaller body sizes than those observed under optimal laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that predators reduce mosquito body size and that predators are present in nature but not in most lab settings.

claim: Smaller mosquito body size is associated with lower reproductive success in mosquitoes.
source: Smaller body size is associated with lower reproductive success in mosquitoes because smaller females lay fewer eggs (Blackmore and Lord, 2000; Lyimo and Takken, 1993; Oliver and Howard, 2011; Styer et al., 2007; Tsunoda et al., 2010), and smaller males produce less sperm (Hatala et al., 2018; Ponlawat and Harrington, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Smaller female mosquitoes lay fewer eggs.
source: Smaller body size is associated with lower reproductive success in mosquitoes because smaller females lay fewer eggs (Blackmore and Lord, 2000; Lyimo and Takken, 1993; Oliver and Howard, 2011; Styer et al., 2007; Tsunoda et al., 2010), and smaller males produce less sperm (Hatala et al., 2018; Ponlawat and Harrington, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Smaller male mosquitoes produce less sperm.
source: Smaller body size is associated with lower reproductive success in mosquitoes because smaller females lay fewer eggs (Blackmore and Lord, 2000; Lyimo and Takken, 1993; Oliver and Howard, 2011; Styer et al., 2007; Tsunoda et al., 2010), and smaller males produce less sperm (Hatala et al., 2018; Ponlawat and Harrington, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Vector lifespan contributes disproportionately to disease transmission.
source: Vector lifespan contributes disproportionately to disease transmission because older vectors are more likely to have been exposed to pathogens, more likely to already be infectious after having survived the extrinsic incubation period, and more likely to survive long enough to bite subsequent hosts (Cator et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cator et al., 2020.

claim: Smaller mosquito body size is associated with shorter mosquito lifespan.
source: It is well-established that smaller mosquito body size is associated with shorter mosquito lifespan (Araújo et al., 2012; Hawley, 1985, Reisen et al., 1984; Reiskind and Lounibos, 2009; Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and stated as well-established knowledge.

claim: Culex pipiens, Culex restuans, and Culex tarsalis all avoid predator habitats.
source: Previous work has shown that Cx. pipiens, Cx. restuans, and Cx. tarsalis all avoid predator habitats (Vonesh and Blaustein, 2010), and that Cx. pipiens is the primary bridge vector of WNV responsible for spill-over transmission from avian reservoir hosts to humans (Fonseca et al., 2004; Hamer et al., 2008a, Kramer et al., 2008; Andreadis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vonesh and Blaustein, 2010.

claim: Culex pipiens is the primary bridge vector of West Nile virus responsible for spill-over transmission from avian reservoir hosts to humans.
source: Previous work has shown that Cx. pipiens, Cx. restuans, and Cx. tarsalis all avoid predator habitats (Vonesh and Blaustein, 2010), and that Cx. pipiens is the primary bridge vector of WNV responsible for spill-over transmission from avian reservoir hosts to humans (Fonseca et al., 2004; Hamer et al., 2008a, Kramer et al., 2008; Andreadis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Culex pipiens mosquitoes can live in permanent aquatic environments such as ground pools, ponds, stream edges, and lake edges.
source: Cx. pipiens mosquitoes can live in permanent aquatic environments, such as ground pools (Amini et al., 2020; Barr, 1967; Dida et al., 2018; Sulesco et al., 2015), ponds (Lühken et al., 2015), stream edges (Amini et al., 2020), and lake edges (Vinogradova, 2000) that are more common in rural areas, but Cx. pipiens are also found in urban and suburban residential areas, where they typically breed in artificial containers (Sulesco et al., 2015), including tires (Lühken et al., 2015; Nikookar et al., 2017; Verna, 2015), rainwater tanks (Townroe and Callaghan, 2014), and catch basins (Gardner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Culex pipiens are found in urban and suburban residential areas where they typically breed in artificial containers.
source: Cx. pipiens mosquitoes can live in permanent aquatic environments, such as ground pools (Amini et al., 2020; Barr, 1967; Dida et al., 2018; Sulesco et al., 2015), ponds (Lühken et al., 2015), stream edges (Amini et al., 2020), and lake edges (Vinogradova, 2000) that are more common in rural areas, but Cx. pipiens are also found in urban and suburban residential areas, where they typically breed in artificial containers (Sulesco et al., 2015), including tires (Lühken et al., 2015; Nikookar et al., 2017; Verna, 2015), rainwater tanks (Townroe and Callaghan, 2014), and catch basins (Gardner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mean dispersal distance of adult Culex mosquitoes is greater than one kilometer.
source: The mean dispersal distance of adult Culex mosquitoes is greater than one kilometer (Ciota et al., 2012; Hamer et al., 2014), and female Cx. pipiens have exhibited longer dispersal distances after developing in the presence of a fish predator (Alcalay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciota et al., 2012 and Hamer et al., 2014.

claim: Female Culex pipiens have exhibited longer dispersal distances after developing in the presence of a fish predator.
source: The mean dispersal distance of adult Culex mosquitoes is greater than one kilometer (Ciota et al., 2012; Hamer et al., 2014), and female Cx. pipiens have exhibited longer dispersal distances after developing in the presence of a fish predator (Alcalay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alcalay et al., 2018.

claim: Drought has been associated with human West Nile virus cases.
source: Drought has previously been associated with human WNV cases (Johnson and Sukhdeo, 2013; Marcantonio et al., 2015; Roehr, 2012; Shaman et al., 2005; Epstein and Defilippo, 2001; Paull et al., 2017), but the association has thus far lacked a clear underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The association between drought and human West Nile virus cases has lacked a clear underlying mechanism.
source: Drought has previously been associated with human WNV cases (Johnson and Sukhdeo, 2013; Marcantonio et al., 2015; Roehr, 2012; Shaman et al., 2005; Epstein and Defilippo, 2001; Paull et al., 2017), but the association has thus far lacked a clear underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current understanding.

claim: Under drought conditions, the density of aquatic organisms increases and predation pressures can intensify.
source: Under drought conditions, the density of aquatic organisms increases and predation pressures can intensify due to compressed space and high encounter rates (Amundrud et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amundrud et al., 2019.

claim: Impacts of fish predation are more severe during the dry season in stream ecosystems.
source: A previous study of a stream ecosystem found that impacts of fish predation are more severe during the dry season (Dudgeon, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dudgeon, 1993.

claim: Mosquitoes respond to a gradient of predator cues.
source: Laboratory and semi-field studies have shown that mosquitoes respond to a gradient of predator cues (Roux et al., 2014; Silberbush and Blaustein, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roux et al., 2014 and Silberbush and Blaustein, 2011.

claim: The frequency of larval anti-predator behavior is correlated with the concentration of predator cues.
source: The frequency of larval anti-predator behavior is correlated with the concentration of predator cues (Roux et al., 2014), and adult female mosquitoes prefer oviposition sites with lower predator densities (Silberbush and Blaustein, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roux et al., 2014.

claim: Adult female mosquitoes prefer oviposition sites with lower predator densities.
source: The frequency of larval anti-predator behavior is correlated with the concentration of predator cues (Roux et al., 2014), and adult female mosquitoes prefer oviposition sites with lower predator densities (Silberbush and Blaustein, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silberbush and Blaustein, 2011.

claim: When suitable oviposition sites are absent, female mosquitoes retain their eggs until sites become available.
source: When suitable oviposition sites are absent, females retain their eggs until sites become available (Bentley and Day, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bentley and Day, 1989.

claim: Culex pipiens females can retain their eggs for up to five weeks.
source: Cx. pipiens females can retain their eggs for up to five weeks, allowing them enough time to find container sites with low predation risk, often located in residential areas (Johnson and Fonseca, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson and Fonseca, 2014.

claim: Vertical transmission of West Nile virus from gravid females to their progeny may occur during oviposition.
source: In addition, vertical transmission of WNV from gravid females to their progeny may occur during oviposition (Rosen, 1988), when the virus is transmitted by an accessory gland fluid that attaches eggs to one another (Nelms et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rosen, 1988 and Nelms et al., 2013.

claim: The rate of vertical transmission in Culex pipiens increases with the number of days following West Nile virus infection.
source: Because the rate of vertical transmission in Cx. pipiens increases with the number of days following WNV infection (Anderson et al., 2008), extended searches for oviposition sites due to drought could increase the frequency of vertical transmission.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2008.

claim: When transmission to an egg raft occurred, only 4.7% of the progeny were found to be infected as adults.
source: However, the impact of vertical transmission on WNV epidemics is thought to be minimal because when transmission to an egg raft did occur, only 4.7% of the progeny were found to be infected as adults (Anderson et al., 2008), and only about half of those infected adults are estimated to be female.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2008.

claim: West Nile virus incidence is more consistently clustered in the Northern Great Plains than in southern Florida.
source: The proposed aggregation of bird and mosquito populations during drought was originally thought to occur in humid, densely vegetated hammocks – a type of habitat that is specific to southern Florida (Shaman et al., 2005), but WNV incidence is more consistently clustered in other regions of the US, particularly the Northern Great Plains (CENTERS FOR DISEASE CONTROL AND PREVENTION, 2021; Sugumaran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to CDC, 2021 and Sugumaran et al., 2009.

claim: Northern cardinals, American robins, and house sparrows were among the bird species that most frequently tested seropositive for West Nile virus antibodies in Chicago in 2005 and 2006.
source: Northern cardinals (Cardinalis cardinalis), American robins (Turdus migratorius), and house sparrows (Passer domesticus) were among the bird species that most frequently tested seropositive for WNV antibodies in 2005 and 2006 in Chicago, where high numbers of human cases were reported (Hamer et al., 2008b), and these passerine species are more abundant in residential areas, regardless of precipitation patterns (Anderson, 2006b; Beddall, 1963; Lepczyk et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hamer et al., 2008b.

claim: Passerine species that are West Nile virus reservoir hosts are more abundant in residential areas, regardless of precipitation patterns.
source: Northern cardinals (Cardinalis cardinalis), American robins (Turdus migratorius), and house sparrows (Passer domesticus) were among the bird species that most frequently tested seropositive for WNV antibodies in 2005 and 2006 in Chicago, where high numbers of human cases were reported (Hamer et al., 2008b), and these passerine species are more abundant in residential areas, regardless of precipitation patterns (Anderson, 2006b; Beddall, 1963; Lepczyk et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson, 2006b; Beddall, 1963; and Lepczyk et al., 2008.

claim: Hatch-year birds are more vulnerable to mosquito biting and contribute to the amplification of West Nile virus.
source: While hatch-year birds are more vulnerable to mosquito biting, and thus contribute to the amplification of WNV (Hamer et al., 2008b), it is illogical to expect an increased abundance of hatch-year birds during drought conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hamer et al., 2008b.

claim: Reductions in hatching success have been observed during drought conditions.
source: Although reductions in both hatching success (George et al., 1992) and survival of recently fledged birds (Yackel Adams et al., 2006) have been observed during drought conditions, the impact of drought on avian abundance varies widely by species (Verner and Purcell, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to George et al., 1992.

claim: Reductions in survival of recently fledged birds have been observed during drought conditions.
source: Although reductions in both hatching success (George et al., 1992) and survival of recently fledged birds (Yackel Adams et al., 2006) have been observed during drought conditions, the impact of drought on avian abundance varies widely by species (Verner and Purcell, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yackel Adams et al., 2006.

claim: The impact of drought on avian abundance varies widely by species.
source: Although reductions in both hatching success (George et al., 1992) and survival of recently fledged birds (Yackel Adams et al., 2006) have been observed during drought conditions, the impact of drought on avian abundance varies widely by species (Verner and Purcell, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Verner and Purcell, 1999.

claim: Synanthropic bird species are less negatively affected by drought.
source: In particular, synanthropic species, such as those likely to harbor WNV, are less negatively affected by drought (Albright et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Albright et al., 2009.

claim: Birds with higher levels of stress hormones are more likely to be fed on by mosquitoes.
source: Finally, birds with higher levels of stress hormones are more likely to be fed on by mosquitoes, and certain factors associated with residential areas, such as road noise, light pollution, and pesticide exposure, can cause avian stress (Gervasi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gervasi et al., 2016.

claim: The aquatic phase of the mosquito life cycle is often overlooked in mathematical models of mosquito-borne pathogen transmission.
source: Although the aquatic phase of the mosquito life cycle is often overlooked in mathematical models of mosquito-borne pathogen transmission (Reiner et al., 2013), vector survival at immature stages plays an important role in determining mosquito population abundance, which is an essential factor for predicting disease transmission (Beck-Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reiner et al., 2013.

claim: Vector survival at immature stages plays an important role in determining mosquito population abundance.
source: Although the aquatic phase of the mosquito life cycle is often overlooked in mathematical models of mosquito-borne pathogen transmission (Reiner et al., 2013), vector survival at immature stages plays an important role in determining mosquito population abundance, which is an essential factor for predicting disease transmission (Beck-Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beck-Johnson et al., 2013.

claim: A biocontrol intervention using copepod predators eliminated Aedes albopictus from three communes in Nam Dinh, Vietnam.
source: For example, a biocontrol intervention relying on the application of copepod predators eliminated Aedes albopictus from three communes in Nam Dinh, Vietnam, where dengue transmission was previously detected, and reduced vector abundance by 86–98% in three other communes (Kay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kay et al., 2002.

claim: A biocontrol intervention using copepod predators reduced Aedes albopictus abundance by 86-98% in three communes in Nam Dinh, Vietnam.
source: For example, a biocontrol intervention relying on the application of copepod predators eliminated Aedes albopictus from three communes in Nam Dinh, Vietnam, where dengue transmission was previously detected, and reduced vector abundance by 86–98% in three other communes (Kay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kay et al., 2002.

claim: The annual abundance of Culex and Anopheles mosquitoes increased 15-fold in semi-permanent wetlands in the year following a drought.
source: Conversely, the annual abundance of Culex and Anopheles mosquitoes was observed to increase 15-fold in semi-permanent wetlands in the year following a drought, likely because the drought eliminated aquatic predators from wetlands that dried completely, and mosquitoes were able to re-colonize newly formed aquatic habitats more quickly than their most effective predators (Chase and Knight, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chase and Knight, 2003.

claim: Predators of vector species can decrease or eliminate pathogen infection in host populations as vector fecundity increases.
source: Previous models have shown that predators of vector species can decrease or eliminate pathogen infection in host populations as vector fecundity increases (Moore et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moore et al., 2010.

claim: The entomological inoculation rate is the product of the number of mosquitoes per host, the daily rate of mosquito biting, and the proportion of mosquitoes that are infectious.
source: The EIR has been defined as the product of three variables: (m) the number of mosquitoes per host, (a) the daily rate of mosquito biting, and (s) the proportion of mosquitoes that are infectious (Beck-Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beck-Johnson et al., 2013.

claim: The relationship between mosquito body size and biting rate is unclear.
source: The relationship between mosquito body size and biting rate is unclear, with some studies showing higher biting rates among larger mosquitoes (Araújo et al., 2012; Gunathilaka et al., 2019), and others reporting higher biting rates among smaller mosquitoes (Farjana and Tuno, 2013; Leisnham et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing contradictory findings.

claim: Some studies show higher biting rates among larger mosquitoes.
source: The relationship between mosquito body size and biting rate is unclear, with some studies showing higher biting rates among larger mosquitoes (Araújo et al., 2012; Gunathilaka et al., 2019), and others reporting higher biting rates among smaller mosquitoes (Farjana and Tuno, 2013; Leisnham et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araújo et al., 2012 and Gunathilaka et al., 2019.

claim: Some studies report higher biting rates among smaller mosquitoes.
source: The relationship between mosquito body size and biting rate is unclear, with some studies showing higher biting rates among larger mosquitoes (Araújo et al., 2012; Gunathilaka et al., 2019), and others reporting higher biting rates among smaller mosquitoes (Farjana and Tuno, 2013; Leisnham et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Farjana and Tuno, 2013 and Leisnham et al., 2008.

claim: Predators play an important role in directly reducing mosquito populations.
source: This meta-analysis on mosquito predation demonstrates that predators not only play an important role in directly reducing mosquito populations, but also have non-consumptive effects on surviving mosquitoes that may ultimately reduce further population growth and decrease disease transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the meta-analysis results.

claim: Predators have non-consumptive effects on surviving mosquitoes that may ultimately reduce further population growth and decrease disease transmission.
source: This meta-analysis on mosquito predation demonstrates that predators not only play an important role in directly reducing mosquito populations, but also have non-consumptive effects on surviving mosquitoes that may ultimately reduce further population growth and decrease disease transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the meta-analysis results.

claim: Predictive disease models are likely to be more reliable when the non-consumptive effects of predation are incorporated.
source: Predictive disease models are likely to be more reliable when the non-consumptive effects of predation are incorporated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the meta-analysis.

claim: Exposure of mosquito larvae to predators remains rare in most laboratory-based assessments of vector traits.
source: Although exposure of mosquito larvae to predators is commonplace in outdoor field settings, it remains rare in most laboratory-based assessments of vector traits.
evidence: This is a general observation about laboratory practices.

claim: Only one study in the database was designed to directly measure the effect of larval-stage predation on vector competence.
source: In the 60-study database that was compiled, only one study was designed to directly measure the effect of larval-stage predation on vector competence (Roux et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a gap in the literature identified during the systematic review.

claim: Two studies from the compiled database examined the compatibility of predators with Bacillus thuringiensis var. israelensis.
source: Two studies from the compiled database examined the compatibility of predators with Bacillus thuringiensis var. israelensis (Bti), a commonly used bacterial biocontrol agent (Chansang et al., 2004; Op de Beeck et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes findings from the systematic review.

claim: Previous studies have supported the simultaneous application of cyclopoid copepod predators and Bti.
source: Previous studies have supported the simultaneous application of cyclopoid copepod predators and Bti (Marten et al., 1993; Tietze et al., 1994), but additional analyses are needed on the use of Bti with other families of mosquito predators.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marten et al., 1993 and Tietze et al., 1994.
